overview.headline: Waste classes decay hazards storage and disposal overview

keyPoints.point: Radioactive waste is a byproduct from reactors at plants and hospitals and research facilities
keyPoints.quote: Radioactive (or nuclear) waste is a byproduct from nuclear reactors, fuel processing plants, hospitals and research facilities.

keyPoints.point: Two broad classifications divide waste into high-level and low-level types
keyPoints.quote: There are two broad classifications: high-level or low-level waste.

keyPoints.point: Strontium and cesium isotopes have half-lives of about 30 years when radioactivity will decay by half
keyPoints.quote: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years (half the radioactivity will decay in 30 years).

keyPoints.point: Spent fuel storage at plant sites is considered temporary before permanent disposal
keyPoints.quote: Spent fuel storage at power plant sites is considered temporary, with the ultimate goal being permanent disposal.

keyTerms.gloss: facilities that use fission to produce energy and generate waste
keyTerms.quote: Radioactive (or nuclear) waste is a byproduct from nuclear reactors, fuel processing plants, hospitals and research facilities.

keyTerms.gloss: waste defined as other than high-level and from medical and industrial sites for disposal
keyTerms.quote: There are two broad classifications: high-level or low-level waste.

keyTerms.gloss: time of about years for half the radioactivity to decay
keyTerms.quote: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years (half the radioactivity will decay in 30 years).

keyTerms.gloss: isotopes created when uranium splits that contribute heat and radiation
keyTerms.quote: These isotopes, called "fission products," account for most of the heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.

keyTerms.gloss: pools of water several feet deep that shield radiation and cool rods
keyTerms.quote: All U.S. nuclear power plants store spent nuclear fuel in "spent fuel pools."
